content: Can someone explain to me why GroupTheory.DoubleCoset has a claim assert_not_exists MonoidWithZero at the beginning? The file still compiles if this sentence is removed. This prevents me from importing GroupTheory.Index
It was added here: #23832
(nevermind, this was a bad idea)
I'd say probably the best course of action is to either remove the assert_not_exists from GroupTheory.DoubleCoset or split GroupTheory.DoubleCoset.
It seems like MonoidWithZero is creeping in through cardinality stuff, so I think MonoidWithZero is probably alright in the group theory library.
Maybe change it to assert_not_exists Field to match other files in the group theory folder?

It's there to prevent you from importing too much, yes. A better solution could be to prevent importing GroupWithZero in GroupTheory.Index too. You'd need to move 7 lemmas about iInf to a new file, and probably index_smul as well.
Didn't look well enough, extricating GroupWithZero from GroupTheory.Index doesn't seem feasible. Probably you can add a new file about DoubleCoset that allows more imports
Why does docs#Subgroup.index need to know about docs#MonoidWithZero ?

Yaël Dillies said:

Why does docs#Subgroup.index need to know about docs#MonoidWithZero ?

Declaration MonoidWithZero is not allowed to be imported by this file.
It is defined in Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.Defs,
  which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.NeZero,
  which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.Basic,
  which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.Units.Basic,
  which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.BigOperators.GroupWithZero.Finset,
  which is imported by Mathlib.GroupTheory.Index,
  which is imported by this file.
Surely the iInf results about index can move to a later file?
Jiaxi, my question is philosophical :wink:
@Yaël Dillies I tried removing the iInf results, but it's much more than that. Nat.card imports MonoidWithZero, so anything about cardinalities in group theory needs MonoidWithZero.
(this was my first instinct too: #mathlib4 > What is `assert_not_exists MonoidWithZero` @ 💬 :slight_smile: )
Ah, right. Nat.card needing MonoidWithZero has been a long-standing issue to me :sad:

Declaration GroupWithZero is not allowed to be imported by this file.
It is defined in Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.Defs,
which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.NeZero,
which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.GroupWithZero.InjSurj,
which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.Order.GroupWithZero.Canonical,
which is imported by Mathlib.Algebra.Order.Ring.Nat,
which is imported by Mathlib.Data.ENat.Monoid,
which is imported by Mathlib.Data.ENat.SuccOrder,
which is imported by Mathlib.Data.ENat.Pow,
which is imported by Mathlib.SetTheory.Cardinal.Finite,
which is imported by this file.
A good first step would be to redefine Nat.card without Cardinal
Hm, now you mention it, I think I did that once

Ruben Van de Velde said:

Didn't look well enough, extricating GroupWithZero from GroupTheory.Index doesn't seem feasible. Probably you can add a new file about DoubleCoset that allows more imports

I don't think this is a good idea. Everything in group theory needs Nat.card, so the proper long-term solution is to redefine Nat.card rather than split files over the import.
Does following the rest of the group theory folder and bumping up to assert_not_exists Field work?

Thomas Browning said:

Does following the rest of the group theory folder and bumping up to assert_not_exists Field work?

assert_not_exists Field works
Weird, I landed #33245 which was part of that work, but I can't find the actual branch
What would be the proposed non-cardinal definition?
Extract it out of a bijection with Fin n, if I recall correctly
https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/compare/master...Ruben-VandeVelde:mathlib4:redefine-nat-card?expand=1
If someone wants to try to get it into shape, have fun :)

Another possibility:

noncomputable example (α : Type*) : ℕ := ⨆ s : Finset α, s.card

not sure if that's better or worse than if h : Finite α then h.exists_equiv_fin.choose else 0 in terms of material required
Oh also could we also get ENat.card/Set.ncard/Set.encard without cardinals while we're at it
Finset.card goes to List.length, so should be pretty light. But how is it to prove with?
If we're going via Finset, would it make sense to start with Set.ncard first?

I guess we could also do

open scoped Classical in
noncomputable example (α : Type*) : ℕ :=
  if h : ∃ n, ∀ l : List α, l.Nodup → l.length ≤ n then Nat.find h else 0

to avoid importing the lattice on Nat, or even this Mathlib-free def:

open scoped Classical in
noncomputable example (α : Type*) : ℕ :=
  if h : ∃ l : List α, l.Nodup ∧ ∀ l' : List α, l'.Nodup → l'.length ≤ l.length then
    h.choose.length
  else 0

but perhaps just using Finite is the best. Both Finite and Nat.find need ~1% of mathlib, which is mostly Data & Logic files which probably don't need Nat.card anyway.
Again, how much work would it be to set up the API with these definitions, and how much extra would you need to import for that?

Okay so I tried both of the definitions that don't require lots of imports (Finite & l.Nodup), without importing Fintype/Finset at all, and both of them seem fine after a slightly annoying "injective → card ≤ card" lemma. This led me to find #9794 which is exactly what we're talking about.

The List def proofs require importing docs#List.Nodup.map, whereas the Finite def proofs require docs#Fin.nonempty_embedding_iff which brings with it a bunch of order theory. Hopefully it's possible to move things around to avoid it.

The more pressing issue IMO is that we'd want to define Nat.card α := (ENat.card α).toNat, but importing docs#ENat.toNat brings lots of order theory and algebra. It was worse before #42271, but even now importing docs#ENat.natCast_toNat also imports MonoidWithZero and even CommRing.

If we can reduce the imports of both docs#ENat.toNat and docs#Fin.nonempty_embedding_iff, I think the Finite def would be great, as it's endorsed by a maintainer.
Also there's a new Basic/ top-level folder, which will hopefully lead to a better overall import hierarchy :)

Can someone give a brief overview of why we care about this issue? As far as I'm concerned, MonoidWithZero is a basic mathematical object, why are we jumping through hoops to avoid it? I know the answer is some more detailed version of "because then some random files early on import less stuff" but why do we care?
To me, the bigger issue is that talking about the cardinality of a type (Nat.card) currently requires going through cardinals and universes (via Cardinal.mk) which is a bit absurd.
We also want to talk about the size of a monoid (or other algebraic objects), but basic monoid files can't import Nat.card unless it avoids importing monoids

Thomas Browning said:

To me, the bigger issue is that talking about the cardinality of a type (Nat.card) currently requires going through cardinals and universes (via Cardinal.mk) which is a bit absurd.

Do you think that proving Fermat's Last Theorem using elliptic curves and modular forms is also a bit absurd? I am trying to understand what the issue is here. I must be missing something fundamental. Who cares what uses what?
Import cycles care

Kevin Buzzard said:

Thomas Browning said:

To me, the bigger issue is that talking about the cardinality of a type (Nat.card) currently requires going through cardinals and universes (via Cardinal.mk) which is a bit absurd.

Do you think that proving Fermat's Last Theorem using elliptic curves and modular forms is also a bit absurd? I am trying to understand what the issue is here. I must be missing something fundamental. Who cares what uses what?

Well, suppose that FLT had an easy elementary proof in terms of modular arithmetic, and that FLT was also used widely in the rest of mathlib. Then it would be a bit absurd to instead prove FLT in mathlib using elliptic curves and modular forms (e.g., it would cause all sorts of import issues, as Snir points out).

So the claim is that the issue is import cycles? And what import cycles are we avoiding by not importing basic cardinal files in files about natural cardinality? For me, basic cardinal files sound like a perfect thing to import early, as cardinals use essentially no mathematics other than stuff like functions and bijections.

There are lots of such basic concepts: Cardinal, Equiv, Function.Embedding, Finite, Fintype, Set, Finset, Multiset, Quotient, Unique, ENat, Relation.ReflTransGen, PartialOrder, Monotone, etc.
We still have to also avoid cycles within them.

Note that currently to use a basic cardinal lemma such as #α ≤ 1 ↔ Subsingleton α you have to import: Monoid, Group, CommRing, big operators, everything on Finset/Fintype/List, the lattice structure on Nat/Multiset/Finset/Set, boolean algebras, (conditionally) complete lattices, Galois connections, Zorn's lemma, etc.
So we're very far from-

Kevin Buzzard said:

cardinals use essentially no mathematics other than stuff like functions and bijections.

There is a friction between basic concepts, and declaring instances on a "basic" type. Due to the nature of files and modules, it has (historically) been easier to kitchen sink imports for the file that defines ENat, so that the deriving line can be the most powerful.

There's not really anything deep going on. We've been experimenting to see if we can build up the basic algebraic theory such that we get the group theory without defining groups with zero, groups with zero without rings, rings without fields... It's not fundamental, but it's interesting to see how far we get
